en: Newly Carved Ten Oxherding Pictures of the Chan School.
Compiled by the Buddhist disciple Jueyin, Hu Wenhuan of Qiantang.
Regarding these Ten Oxherding Pictures: they are metaphors employed by the Chan school for the purpose of cultivating the mind and realizing the Way. The Cowherd...
The ox is the person; the radiant halo is the human mind. When both are completely integrated and transformed, one realizes the Way of original suchness.
Now, who does not possess a mind? Since all possess it, all ought to cultivate it. And who does not embody the Way? Since all embody it, all ought to realize it.
If one possesses [these conditions], all shall surely realize it. Yet, is this merely an analogy for the Chan school?
Even our Confucianism is no different. Is it only our Confucianism that is the same? Even all people in the world are likewise the same.
In essence, there is no difference from beginning to end; the principle is exceedingly clear. It is only because they are obscured by worldly desires that they willingly follow the ox.
It is merely that one has not yet done so. Now, even an ox can be tamed; it has never been the case that the mind cannot be cultivated.
Nor has it ever been the case that, though the mind can be cultivated, the Way cannot be realized. Furthermore, if the Way is said to be inherently present, why would the mind require cultivation?
It is because of the obscuration of sensory desires. Therefore, I have selected these ten oxen.

I have further appended this "Diagram of the Causes and Conditions of Suffering and Pleasure" so that people may understand the origins of material desires and strive diligently to overcome them, thereby realizing their original nature.
These two diagrams appear to emerge from a single analogy, yet the analogy itself does not transcend a single principle.
Those who contemplate them will clearly gain insight; if they expand and apply this understanding, it will be as if—
To say, "My own body is also like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, a dewdrop, or a flash of lightning"—what, then, is this [body] being compared to?
That which does not depend on returning to the origin and does not require recourse to metaphors is the Supreme Vehicle. Alas!
Those who fall below this level should also strive toward it.
Puming’s Verse on the Unbroken Herd:
Born wild, its horns and head are fierce as it bellows at will; It gallops along mountain paths and by streams, growing ever more distant.
A single mass of black clouds hangs across the mouth of the valley— Who knows that with every step it tramples the fine grain?
Yun’an’s verse on "The Mind of Unherded Wildness":
With a wild mind and vigorous strength, one roars and bellows incessantly; The peace and stability of the realm grow ever more distant.
Rushing recklessly through perils and heights, Who at any time considers the people’s grain?
Puming’s First Verse:
I have a thorny rope passed through my nose; With every rush toward competition, I am struck with a whip.
My naturally inferior nature has long been difficult to tame, Yet I am still led by the strength of a mountain boy.
Yun’an’s verse on the initial training of a dark-hued horse:
Its entire body is covered in fine hair, and its nostrils have just been pierced; If you wish to control it when it is difficult to manage, do not fail to apply the whip.
I send word to the cowherd: you must exert all your strength, And ensure the tethering rope is pulled tight once more.
Puming’s Verse: Restrained and gradually tamed, the wild gallop is stilled; crossing waters and piercing clouds, he follows step by step.
Grasping the tangle-rope with no slackening, the cowherd boy forgets his fatigue throughout the day.
Yun’an’s *Hezhi* (Verses on Restraint):
The mind races, yet it must not race recklessly; I pull firmly on the nose-rope, and we follow one another closely.
With its bony head and horns now sunk within the moat and trench, I still regret that the strength of the young boy has not yet failed.
Puming’s Verse on Returning the Gaze:
After long practice, the merit deepens and one finally turns the head; The wild mind’s power gradually becomes supple and gentle.
The mountain boy is not yet willing to grant full permission; He still holds the thorny rope to bind him fast.
Yun’an and Huíshǒu:
The Ox Herding—The Ox Has Already Turned Its Head Back. A hundredfold tempering makes steel supple as it bends;
The spring river’s emerald green stirs waves of sorrow, Yet the tattered rope remains to tether it.
Puming’s Verse on Taming [the Ox]:
Beneath the shade of ancient willows by the stream, Letting go and gathering back comes naturally.
At twilight, amidst green clouds and fragrant grasslands, The cowherd boy returns; there is no need to lead him by the rope.
Yun’an’s Tamed and Submissive [Horse]:
Beside the clear waters at the head of the fragrant grasslands, Under willow shade where the sands are warm, he strides with serene detachment.
His frost-white coat is already half-plump and glossy; He follows his master in submission, needing no rein to lead him.
Puming’s Verse on Unimpeded Ease:
Sleeping soundly in the open field, the mind is as it wishes; Without the toil of whip or spur, forever free from constraint.
The mountain boy sits steadily beneath the green pines; A single melody of peace and prosperity is more than enough.
Yun’an’s Verse on Wu’ai:
The white ox lies peacefully, its body as it is; The six gates are empty and still, entirely unconfined.
The herdsman beneath the pines blows a single tune; Its resonance harmonizes with the wind, leaving nothing behind.
Puming’s Verse on Spontaneity:

Amidst the evening glow upon the spring waves by the willow bank, Where thin mist and lush green grass form a verdant carpet, One passes the time eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty; Upon the mountain rock, the stone boy sleeps soundly.
In Yun’an’s poem: Amidst the shallow waters and sandy banks, all is left to its natural course; A single glance reveals the lush, verdant grasses of the gauze-skirted fields.
Beneath the willow shade, children sleep while the oxen graze; Who would ask if the springtime radiance is as potent as wine?
Puming’s Verse on Mutual Forgetting:
The white ox is ever present amidst the white clouds; Man is naturally mindless, and the ox is the same.
The moon pierces the white clouds, casting white shadows; Let the white clouds and bright moon drift as they will toward the west or east.
In Yun’an’s verse: Man and ox forget each other within the marshy lands; Leisurely they go and come, sharing the same nature as water and clouds.
Tranquil, they no longer compare themselves to fish in the river; The moon flows from the west as the sun rises in the east.
Puming’s Verse: The solitary ox shines alone;
nowhere is there a cowherd to tend it. A single drifting cloud amidst the azure peaks;
Clapping hands and singing aloud beneath the bright moon— Yet upon returning, there remains yet one more barrier.
Yun’an’s verse on “The Ox Forgets the Herdsman”:
With hat and staff, there is leisure beyond measure; Moon bright and wind clear within heaven and earth.
Reaching this point, it is as if a single thread has been passed through; Naturally, one treads upon the pass above.
Puming’s Verse on the Mutual Extinction of Man and Ox:
Neither man nor ox is seen; their traces are utterly lost. The bright moonlight is cold, and the myriad phenomena are empty.
If you ask for the essential meaning within this, Wild flowers and fragrant grasses grow in dense clusters of their own accord.
In Yun’an’s verse on the "Double Extinction of Oxen and Children," all traces of movement are severed; It is clearly manifest like space, yet not empty space.
It is as if within the springtime of a great peace, Where the secluded birds still sing among the fragrant thickets.
In the past, King Udayana questioned the Venerable Piṇḍola: "How does one practice within the Buddha-dharma?
The Venerable replied, "It is like a person traveling through a vast wilderness amidst a great conflagration who is then attacked by a mad elephant."
The man pursued was seen by another person standing beside a well where there was a tree with a creeper upon it. The man grasped the creeper and hung above the well;
below were three venomous dragons and four poisonous snakes. On the tree were a black and a white mouse that gnawed at the creeper from opposite sides.
Furthermore, around the perimeter were venomous bees stinging him. At that moment, a few drops of honey fell into his mouth.
Because of his craving for the honey, he consequently forgot his suffering. The King asked again, "Does this person experience more suffering or more happiness?
The Venerable One replied, "This person consists entirely of the nature of suffering; what happiness could there be? Those who possess wisdom explain such matters through analogies.
Thereupon, a verse was spoken:
Two rats gnaw at the vine—truly a hundred sufferings; Four snakes surround the well—further a thousand anxieties.
Suddenly they bite through the root of the vine; When will one sink and emerge with head above?
Furthermore, that vast wilderness is the triple world (*tridhātu*). The tree is the body of suffering. Its constant engagement in the activities of various sufferings is inconceivable.
The climbing vine is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The elephant is the murderous demon of impermanence (*anityatā*).
The two rats, black and white, are the revolving sun and moon. The well is the path to the Yellow Springs (the underworld). The three dragons are... [text ends]
Greed, hatred, and delusion are the three poisons. They create the three evil realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The four snakes are the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind; they are also the four non-virtues: alcohol, sensual desire, wealth, and anger;
and they are also the four gates: birth, old age, sickness, and death. "The hand grasping the vine" refers to ignorance. "Honey" refers to husband and wife. "Lustful desire" [is what follows].
Sentimental attachment stains the mind. The mind is fire, and the body is its dwelling. People do not realize that this burning house of theirs is a place where all manner of suffering accumulates.
Day and night they are tormented by it, yet they crave only affection and love. Once the life-root is severed, one falls forever into the depths of samsara.
Having once lost this human form, it will be difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas. I earnestly exhort everyone to take advantage of this healthy physical body.
Stealing leisure from the midst of busyness, every day at dawn and dusk, single-mindedly recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" a thousand or ten thousand times.
In this life, long-term blessings will increase and calamities will be dispelled; at the moment of death, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. The Verse says:
When the wisteria snaps and one falls into the well, life is hard to escape; If elephants, rats, and snakes attack, the hands must be firmly secured.
Take Amida as your own; hope for early awakening, And do not let yourself encounter the bitter realms of the three evil paths.
Fatty foods, sweets, wine, and meat are like honey mixed with arsenic; Loving spouses are knives hidden within a smile.
I exhort all people of the world to reflect with great urgency, lest today turn once more into tomorrow.
Hu Wen-huan, having finished viewing the painting of the ox, realized it clearly: Upon further reflection, suffering and joy have their causes and conditions.
Even if one’s original nature were not empty, Ultimately, the perfect radiance would not manifest before one.
If one breaks through the Zen mechanism and finds the Buddha within the mind, One departs from the evil realms and harbors a heaven within the belly.
Know that this is not a difficult matter; Try applying the whip of diligent effort. (End)
